The Aristotle's catfish, Silurus aristotelis, is a freshwater species endemic to the Acheloos River basin in Greece. Research indicates that females typically reach a total length of 23 cm [Lp = 23 cm] at the onset of puberty, a size that marks the initiation of gonadal development. The ultimate total length attained by this species has been documented at 46 cm [Li = 46 cm], a relatively modest maximum size compared to its larger congener, the European wels catfish. Following external fertilisation and a brief incubation period, the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion. At the time of hatchling emergence, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low at approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], a value that reflects the small diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs typical of this silurid. This minimal mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding to sustain the actively growing larva during the pelagic larval phase. The embryonic development leading up to this stage is temperature-dependent, with the optimal hatching and growth parameters recorded at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
